title: The House of Old Chapel Road
premise: Folklorist Juniper Almeida returns to her late grandmother's house on Old Chapel Road to archive a cycle of village songs that no one will sing twice, discovering that each song was once a binding — and that her grandmother's recordings kept something in the cellar politely seated. When Juniper's documentation work accidentally unbinds the oldest verse, an invited guest takes its place at the table, appearing as an extra chair in every photograph taken in the house. To survive until sunrise, Juniper must choose between the duty of preserving the songs intact and the truth that her grandmother deliberately left one verse unfinished out of love for someone who never came home. She finishes the verse herself, sings it twice, and sends the guest back — but keeps one recording, because some prayers should be answered again.
about_author: Wren Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories in coastal farming towns before turning to fiction. They write horror about the things families keep in filing cabinets.

chapters.title: The Songs No One Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Juniper arrives on Old Chapel Road with recording equipment and her grandmother's key, interviewing villagers who go silent mid-verse. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: the ache of homecoming shadowed by the village's practiced evasions.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Dead Woman's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Juniper catalogs the house, finding labeled tapes, salt lines under doorframes, and a dining set with chairs that don't match the family photos. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: grief braided with the first cold prickle of wrongness.

chapters.title: Tape Seven
chapters.summary: Playing her grandmother's seventh tape, Juniper hears a voice answer the singer — a voice not on any known track. The tape ends mid-word. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: scholarly excitement curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Counts Chairs
chapters.summary: Elderly neighbor Tomas warns her to count the chairs every night and never sit in the extra one. He won't say whose chair it is. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being the only one willing to ask questions.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Remember
chapters.summary: Digitizing old family albums, Juniper finds that recent scans of decades-old photos now include a high-backed chair no one remembers. In the newest picture, it has moved closer to the table. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: vertigo — the past is being edited in real time.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Verse
chapters.summary: In grandmother's papers, Juniper finds the full song cycle transcribed except its final verse, which stops after two lines. A margin note reads: 'Leave him room.' POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: suspicion that love and cowardice wore the same handwriting.

chapters.title: Village of Polite Silence
chapters.summary: Juniper presses the choir mistress, who finally admits the songs were sung twice only once — in 1968, the night the Halloran boy vanished. POV: alternating Juniper and choir mistress. Emotional beat: collective guilt pressing down like weather.

chapters.title: The Cellar Has Good Acoustics
chapters.summary: Following the tape's ambient sound, Juniper locates the recording spot: the cellar, where the walls are scored with tally marks and a place is set at a small table below the floorboards. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing documentation led her exactly where she was meant to go.

chapters.title: An Invitation, Properly Extended
chapters.summary: Juniper realizes her own field recordings — played aloud in the house — constituted an invitation. That night, every clock in the house stops at 3:12. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: self-blame sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Chair Arrives
chapters.summary: A new photograph develops with the chair pulled fully up to the kitchen table, a place setting laid, steam rising from an empty cup. The house smells of someone else's cooking. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: terror domesticated — the worst things arrive politely.

chapters.title: Rules of Hospitality
chapters.summary: Juniper researches folklore of bound guests and threshold law: what is invited may be fed but not named, housed but not thanked. She drafts survival rules on the kitchen wall. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: fragile control through ritual and scholarship.

chapters.title: Halloran's Boy
chapters.summary: Tomas confesses: the vanished boy was his brother, lured by a song sung twice as a dare. Grandmother finished the binding alone and paid for it with her voice. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: fifty years of complicity breaking open.

chapters.title: The Guest at Supper
chapters.summary: At dusk the chair is occupied — a figure like a young man made of pause and echo, waiting to be acknowledged. Juniper serves it bread without looking up. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: courage as sheer refusal to flinch.

chapters.title: It Knows Her Name
chapters.summary: The guest speaks in stitched-together voices from the tapes, including her grandmother's, offering to trade truths for thanks. Juniper nearly says 'thank you' before catching herself. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: the seduction of grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: A hidden letter reveals grandmother loved the thing in the cellar once — or loved the boy it used to be — and left the verse unfinished so he'd always have a seat. Duty said bind; love said leave room. POV: grandmother (letter) / Juniper. Emotional beat: heartbreak reframing the haunting as mercy.

chapters.title: Midnight Census
chapters.summary: The house begins rearranging itself toward hospitality: doors opening inward, beds making themselves, the table growing longer. Juniper counts chairs — eleven, twelve, thirteen. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: claustrophobic escalation as the house chooses its guest over its heir.

chapters.title: The Second Singing
chapters.summary: Juniper understands the binding requires the final verse sung twice by blood. But singing it completed might free the boy rather than banish him — and freeing him means losing the protection that keeps the worse thing beneath the floor fed. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: the impossible arithmetic of mercy.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Below the floor, the true hunger stirs — the guest is not the danger but the seal. The photographs begin showing a second chair, then a third. Sunrise is two hours off. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: dawning scale of the mistake, and of her grandmother's sacrifice.

chapters.title: Two Lines and a Promise
chapters.summary: Juniper descends to the cellar table, sits across from the guest, and sings the unfinished two lines as written — an offering, not a binding. The guest weeps with borrowed voices. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: tenderness inside terror; the climax begins as communion.

chapters.title: Sunrise Arithmetic
chapters.summary: As light touches the windows, Juniper completes the verse in her own words — trading her grandmother's silence for her own voice — and sings it twice. The guest stands, bows, and becomes a boy, then a memory, then nothing. The second chairs collapse into splinters. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: catharsis; love paying duty's debt in full.

chapters.title: After the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Days later, the house is quiet, the photographs ordinary, the clocks running. The village sings once, together, and stops — but this time by choice, not fear. Tomas brings flowers for two graves. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: mourning that has become gratitude.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Juniper archives everything — including one unlabeled tape she records herself, addressed to whoever inherits the house. She leaves a chair by the window, just in case, and locks the door behind her. POV: Juniper. Emotional beat: bittersweet coda; some invitations are how we keep faith with the dead.
